definitions.text: Not produced by labor or toil. "Unlabored harvests." Dryden.
Not cultivated; untitled; as, an unlabored field.
Not laboriously produced, or not evincing labor; as, an unlabored style or work. Tickell.
To loose by undoing a lacing; as, to unlace a shoe.
To loose the dress of; to undress; hence, to expose; to disgrace. What's the matter, That you unlace your reputation thus Shak.
(Naut.)
To loose, and take off, as a bonnet from a sail, or to cast off, as any lacing in any part of the rigging of a vessel. Totten.
To take the load from; to take out the cargo of; as, to unlade a ship or a wagon. The venturous merchant . . . Shall here unlade him and depart no more. Dryden.
To unload; to remove, or to have removed, as a load or a burden; to discharge. There the ship was to unlade her burden. Acts. xxi. 3.
Not laid or placed; not fixed. Hooker.
Not allayed; not pacified; not laid finally to rest. [R.] "Stubborn, unlaid ghost." Milton.
Not laid out, as a corpse. [R.] B. Jonson. Unlaid paper. See Laid paper, under Laid.
To deprive of lands.
To unfold. [Obs.] Wyclif.
To loose, as that which is lashed or tied down.
To open or loose by lifting the latch; as, to unlatch a door.
To recall, as former laughter. [Obs. & R.] Sir T. More.
To deprive of the authority or character of law. [Obs.]
To put beyond protection of law; to outlaw. [Obs.]
(Scots Law)
To impose a fine upon; to fine.
Not having the claws and balls of the forefeet cut off; -- said of dogs.
Not according to law; being or done in violation of law; unlawful. Milton.
To untwist; as, to unlay a rope.
To forget, as what has been learned; to lose from memory; also, to learn the contrary of. I had learned nothing right; I had to unlearn everything. Milner.
To fail to learn. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
Not learned; untaught; uneducated; ignorant; illiterate.
Not gained by study; not known.
Not exhibiting learning; as, unlearned verses.
To free from a leash, or as from a leash; to let go; to release; as, to unleash dogs.
Not leavened; containing no leaven; as, unleavened bread.

Upon any less condition than (the fact or thing stated in the sentence or clause which follows); if not; supposing that not; if it be not; were it not that; except; as, we shall fail unless we are industrious. frequently used prepositionally, -- a construction common in Shakespeare and still employed colloquially. Here nothing breeds unless the nightly owl. Shak.
Not like; dissimilar; diverse; having no resemblance; as, the cases are unlike.
Not likely; improbable; unlikely. [Obsoles.] Unlike quantities (Math.), quantities expressed by letters which are different or of different powers, as a, b, c, a2, a3, xn, and the like.
Absence of likelihood.
The quality or state of being unlikely.
Not likely; improbable; not to be reasonably expected; as, an unlikely event; the thing you mention is very unlikely.
Not holding out a prospect of success; likely to fail; unpromising; as, unlikely means. Hooker.
Not such as to inspire liking; unattractive; disagreeable. [Obs.] "The unlikely eld of me." Chaucer.
In an unlikely manner.
To make unlike; to dissimilate. [Obs.] Wyclif.
The quality or state of being unlike; want of resemblance; dissimilarity. Tennyson.
To detach the limber from; as, to unlimber a gun.
Illimitable. Locke.
Not limited; having no bounds; boundless; as, an unlimited expanse of ocean.
Undefined; indefinite; not bounded by proper exceptions; as, unlimited terms. "Nothing doth more prevail than unlimited generalities." Hooker.

Unconfined; not restrained; unrestricted. Ascribe not unto God such an unlimited exercise of mercy as may destroy his justice. Rogers. Unlimited problem (Math.), a problem which is capable of an infinite number of solutions.
To take the lining out of; hence, to empty; as, to unline one's purse.
To separate or undo, as links; to uncoil; to unfasten. Shak.
Not liquidated; not exactly ascertained; not adjusted or settled. Unliquidated damages (Law), penalties or damages not ascertained in money. Burrill.
Not moistened or wet with liquor; dry. "Unliquored coach." Bp. Hall.
Not in liquor; not intoxicated; sober. Like an unliquored Silenus. Milton.
Not listed; specif. (New York Stock Exchange),
admitted to quotation in the unlisted department, that is, admitted to be dealt in on the floor, but not to the "regular list."
To [R.] Glanvill.
Bereft or deprived of life. [Obs.] Shak.
To take the load from; to discharge of a load or cargo; to disburden; as, to unload a ship; to unload a beast.
Hence, to relieve from anything onerous.
To discharge or remove, as a load or a burden; as, to unload the cargo of a vessel.
To draw the charge from; as, to unload a gun.
To sell in large quantities, as stock; to get rid of. [Brokers' Cant, U. S.]
To perform the act of unloading anything; as, let unload now.
One who, or that which, unloads; a device for unloading, as hay from a wagon.
Not located or placed; not fixed in a place.
Not surveyed, or designated by marks, limits, or boundaries, as appropriated to some individual, company, or corporation; as, unlocated lands.
To unfasten, as what is locked; as, to unlock a door or a chest.
To open, in general; to lay open; to undo. Unlock your springs, and open all your shades. Pope. [Lord] unlock the spell of sin. J. H. Newman.
To dislodge; to deprive of lodgment. Carew.
To recall or retract, as a look. [R.] Richardson.
Not observed or foreseen; unexpected; -- generally with for. "Unlooked success." Denham. She comes unlooked for, if she comes at all. Pope.
Not looked for; unexpected; as, an unlooked-for event.
To make loose; to loosen; to set free. Shak.
To become unfastened; to lose all connection or union.
To loosen; to unloose.
To deprive of the rank or position of a lord. Milton.
Etym: [Properly p. p. of unlord.]
Deprived of the rank of a lord.
Etym: [Pref. un- + lorded.]
Not raised to the rank of a lord. Milton.
To cease to love; to hate. [Obs.]
Not lovely; not amiable; possessing qualities that excite
In an unlucky manner.
Quality or state of being unlucky.

Not lucky; not successful; unfortunate; ill-fated; unhappy; as, an unlucky man; an unlucky adventure; an unlucky throw of dice; an unlucky game. results from chance or fortuity, as in games of hazard, rather than from lack or feebleness of effort.
Bringing bad luck; ill-omened; inauspicious. Haunt me not with that unlucky face. Dryden.
Mischievous; as, an unlucky wag. [Colloq.]
Listlessness; disinclination. [Obs.] "Idleness and unlust." Chaucer.
To separate, as things cemented or luted; to take the lute or the clay from. Boyle.
